newsitem.title: USA: U.S. Gulf remains flush with foreign crude offers.
newsitem.headline: U.S. Gulf remains flush with foreign crude offers.

text.p: U.S. Gulf Coast refiners continue to enjoy an array of choices when looking to fill their needs, with West African and North Sea crudes on offer in competition with domestic grades, traders said Thursday.
"There are still some cargoes left unsold for the Brent," said a foreign crude trader.
He noted West African and North Sea cargoes were offered at weak prices, with talk putting Brent for mid-April delivery at May West Texas Intermediate/Cushing minus 60-70 cents.
North Sea wet deals on Thursday consisted on just one trade, a March 29-31 cargo at April Brent -90 cents, steady to weaker from recent trades.
Traders were not positive if the Brent on offer remained from the batch of supply Swiss traders Glencore brought to the coast recently.
Latin American cargoes were also on offer, with prices steady in recent sessions for a Cano Limon cargo pegged for early April delivery at May WTI -$3.25 FOB.
Trading sources said they expected the excess foreign crudes to be absorbed in the coming weeks, possibly leading to a short-term crunch.
"If these floods in Louisiana cause problems for pipelines, then you could see, in maybe a week or 10 days people wondering why May/June Brent is at plus 40 cts," said a trader.
Mississippi River flooding caused headaches for barge traffic on Thursday, with swaths of the great river shut between Baton Rouge and New Orleans, La. for chunks of the day.
Crude traders said there were whispers of flooding problems for some pipelines, possibly putting some operations under water, according to one source.
U.S. aftermarket Brent paper trades saw May Brent outrights sell numerous times for small parcels totalling around two-and-a-half cargoes at softer prices.
Inter-month spreads moved in the April/May at plus 12 and 13 cts, traders said.
